name: Dermabrasion
lead: Dermabrasion is a surgical skin-planing procedure in which a dermatologist or plastic surgeon mechanically wears away the upper to mid layers of skin to smooth acne scars, deep surgical scars and other surface irregularities.[1] As the skin heals it re-forms from deeper structures, which is how people use it to get a smoother, more even facial surface.[1][9] It is distinct from microdermabrasion, a lighter non-invasive exfoliation done in salons and at home.[1][10]

Wikipedia states that ablative lasers such as CO2 and Er:YAG have largely replaced dermabrasion because they cause less bleeding and depend less on operator skill, though dermabrasion remains in use, partly because it may cost less and can match or exceed laser results for some conditions, a point it supports with a 1998 minipig comparison.[1] Grokipedia describes it as best suited to lighter Fitzpatrick skin types and reports benefits that may wane after two to three years.[9]

Research on dermabrasion today consists mostly of small comparisons with other resurfacing methods, studies in vitiligo and stretch marks, and technique reviews in plastic-surgery journals.[2][11][14][16][17] In looksmaxxing forums the word often refers to microneedling or derma-stamp devices rather than surgical dermabrasion.[8]

chain: A surgeon abrades the upper to mid layers of skin under local anaesthesia
The skin re-epithelialises over 1 to 4 weeks
Acne and surgical scars sit shallower and the surface looks smoother
angle.text: Dermabrasion levels raised or pitted scar tissue by removing surface layers so new skin forms over a smoother base. It is used on the face for acne scars and surgical scars, and in selected cases for fine lines and sun damage.

paras: The procedure is usually done under local anaesthesia in a surgical suite or medical centre. Tools described include wire brushes, diamond wheels, sterilised sandpaper and salt crystals, and minor bleeding is typical.[1] Grokipedia describes a handheld dermabrader with a diamond fraise, wire brush or serrated wheel, with the surgeon working to the point of pinpoint bleeding, which it associates with the papillary dermis.[9]

Indications named in reference sources include deeper acne scars, deep surgical and traumatic scars, birthmarks, superficial tattoos, sun damage, fine perioral and periorbital wrinkles, actinic keratoses and rhinophyma.[1][9] Wikipedia describes it as removing the upper to mid skin layers, whereas laser resurfacing and microneedling work by different mechanisms.[1]

Grokipedia reports that afterwards the area is covered with saline-soaked gauze and an occlusive ointment, that re-epithelialisation typically takes 7 to 14 days, that redness can last up to two months, and that full colour normalisation can take three months or longer.[9] It lists daily broad-spectrum sun protection for 6 to 12 months and a return to work after about two weeks, and mentions a follow-up within 48 to 72 hours to check for infection.[9] Wikipedia gives an overall healing range of about 7 to 30 days.[1] Specific aftercare is set by the treating clinician.

Grokipedia credits German dermatologist Ernst Kromayer with the first motorised dermabrasion in 1905, using rotating burrs for post-acne scarring; American plastic surgeon Percy Iverson with using sandpaper for traumatic facial tattoos in 1947; and New York dermatologist Abner Kurtin with the modern high-speed rotary technique, using wire brushes or diamond fraises, in 1953.[9] It also credits E. H. Hermans with describing diamond fraises for better control in 1957 and says guidelines on timing and aftercare were standardised in the 1990s, though it contains internal inconsistencies on the diamond-fraise dates.[9] These dates come from an AI-generated reference and are listed here as attributed.

By the 1990s ablative lasers entered scar resurfacing; a 1996 study examined a high-energy pulsed CO2 laser for atrophic facial acne scars, the type of scar for which dermabrasion had been the standard.[3] Microdermabrasion, a separate lighter technique, was developed in Italy in 1985, received its first FDA approval letter in 1996 and was first sold in the US in January 1997.[10]

Microdermabrasion removes only the outermost stratum corneum with crystals, diamond tips, bristle tips or water spray, often with suction. Sessions last 5 to 60 minutes with little downtime, results are temporary, and it is typically repeated every two to four weeks; it is used for superficial hyperpigmentation, fine lines and shallow acne scars.[10] Home kits and 'hydradermabrasion' variants also exist.[10]

Clinical studies have tested modified forms of dermabrasion, including electrofulguration-assisted and electrodermabrasion compared with manual dermabrasion,[15][19] and dermabrasion used to prepare skin for cell-suspension transplantation in vitiligo.[13][14][15] Microneedling and derma-stamp devices create micro-injuries to stimulate healing and are reported to be used for rolling and atrophic acne scars across skin types, with about one to two days of swelling, according to Grokipedia.[9]

A review of acne scar pathogenesis, classification and treatment discusses resurfacing among the treatment options for different scar types.[2] A 1996 study examined a high-energy pulsed CO2 laser for atrophic acne scars.[3] A 2010 clinical trial examined dermabrasion for acne scars during treatment with oral isotretinoin.[12] A randomised, single-blind trial in 48 women compared galvano-puncture and dermabrasion with a control group for stretch marks on the buttocks, measuring the length and width of the largest stria with a caliper.[11]

In vitiligo, randomised trials have compared dermabrasion with 5-fluorouracil against suction blister (2021), dermabrasion against microneedling for cell-suspension transplantation (2023) and electrofulguration-assisted against manual dermabrasion (2022).[13][14][15] Registered trials include a split-scar trial of dermabrasion on Mohs surgery wounds (29 participants, 2025), a comparison of laser resurfacing and dermabrasion for scar revision (6 participants), a trial comparing microneedling with dermabrasion for early facial scars (30 participants, recruiting), a trial of tretinoin versus superficial dermabrasion for stretch marks (32 participants), and a planned trial of dermabrasion for free-flap aesthetic enhancement.[4][5][6][7][18] Technique overviews appeared in Clinics in Plastic Surgery (2011) and Facial Plastic Surgery (2014).[16][17]

Wikipedia lists scarring, skin discoloration, infection, reactivation of cold sores and bleeding, which can be heavy in aggressive cases. Lasers are described as causing little or no bleeding and being less operator-dependent.[1] Grokipedia adds that dyspigmentation is more common in darker skin, that hypertrophic or keloid scarring can occur, and that prolonged redness is possible.[9]
Microdermabrasion is described as usually minimal in risk: temporary dryness, sun sensitivity and rarely bruising or scratches, with eye and inhalation precautions for crystal systems.[10]

On looksmax.org the term appears mainly in discussions of skin and scalp microneedling. One thread asks whether members use derma stamps or 'dermabrasion' for skin or scalp microneedling; one reply describes using a motorised pen device a few times a month, and another reply says cheaper pens are adequate for the scalp.[8] The thread concerns microneedling tools rather than surgical dermabrasion.[8]

Scar-focused skin improvement is a recurring theme in looksmaxxing alongside tretinoin, chemical peels, lasers and microneedling, and surgical dermabrasion is usually described there as the older, deeper procedure that dermatologists and plastic surgeons perform.[1][8]

Human studies are mostly small comparisons: dermabrasion for acne scars during isotretinoin treatment,[12] versus galvano-puncture for stretch marks,[11] and in vitiligo cell-transplant protocols.[13][14][15] Registered trials continue to compare dermabrasion with microneedling and laser resurfacing.[5][6] Published results from several registrations have not been reported.[4][5][6][7]

claims.experts: Reference sources describe surgical dermabrasion as removing upper to mid skin layers under local anaesthesia, distinct from microneedling, which creates micro-injuries.[1][9]

claims.experts: Dermabrasion has long been used for deeper acne scars, and reviews discuss resurfacing alongside lasers and other options; lasers have largely replaced it.[1][2][3]

claims.believers: Advocates cite lower cost and operator experience.[1]

card.summary: Surgical sanding of scars, the older standard that lasers largely replaced; sources here mostly small trials.
card.note: Invasive; scarring, discoloration and infection are reported risks.

quick.overview:
Dermabrasion is a surgical procedure that abrades the upper to mid skin layers, mainly to reduce acne and surgical scars.

Wikipedia says lasers have largely replaced it, though it remains in use.
quick.mechanism: Wire brushes, diamond wheels or similar tools remove skin layers under local anaesthesia; healing takes roughly 7 to 30 days.
quick.risks: Reported complications include scarring, discoloration, infection, cold-sore reactivation and bleeding.
